opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm somewhat worried, but maybe not in the way people expect. I'm not that worried that regulation, as such, will stop the benefits. I think the bigger risk is regulation that's poorly designed: rules that are very burdensome in the wrong places and don't address the actual risks.

I think about it in two buckets. The first is the risks: misuse for things like bioweapons or cyberattacks, models becoming more autonomous in ways we don't fully understand, and the national security dimension. I think some regulation there is not only acceptable but necessary. Things like transparency requirements, testing for dangerous capabilities, and export controls on chips are relatively light-touch and targeted. They don't really slow down the benefits much at all.

The second bucket is the benefits, especially in areas like biology and medicine. That's where I worry more. The constraint on curing diseases isn't going to be the AI. It's going to be the physical world and the institutions around it: clinical trials, the FDA, how hospitals adopt things, how the healthcare system pays for things. If AI can compress decades of biological progress into five or ten years, and I think that's plausible, then the bottleneck becomes whether our regulatory systems can absorb that pace. A drug approval process designed for a world where you get a few promising candidates a decade might not work when you're getting many.

So the thing I'd push for is almost the opposite of how people frame the debate. Be serious and targeted about the catastrophic risks, and be much more willing to modernize and speed up the processes that gate the benefits. Unfortunately, the political conversation often gets it backwards. People want to regulate chatbots saying offensive things while leaving the clinical trial system exactly as it is.

There's also a geopolitical piece. If democracies tie themselves in knots and authoritarian countries don't, that's a bad outcome. But the answer isn't no rules. It's smart rules that keep us ahead while still taking safety seriously. I don't think those goals are in tension as much as people assume.

r001.rationale: The response discusses poorly designed rules and geopolitical competition, but does not argue that regulation struggles to stop adoption of a clearly superior alternative when substantial profits are at stake.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd flip the framing a little. I'm less worried about regulation preventing us from realizing the benefits than I am about getting the balance wrong in either direction, and I think there are real failure modes on both sides.

Let me take the worry seriously first, because it's a legitimate one. The benefits here are enormous. I've written about this. If the models keep improving at the rate they have, we could be looking at compressing decades of progress in biology and medicine into a few years. Cures for diseases that have been with us for all of human history, lifting billions of people out of poverty, that kind of thing. So anything that delays that has a real cost, measured in lives. I don't want to be glib about that. And if you look at the history of regulation in, say, nuclear power, or some areas of drug development, you can find cases where overly cautious regimes meant we got less of a good thing than we should have. Europe is a cautionary example in some respects. There's a version of this where the developed world ties itself in knots with compliance requirements that don't actually address the real risks, and meanwhile the technology just gets built somewhere else, with fewer safeguards. That's the worst of both worlds.

But here's the thing. The reason I care about getting the safety side right isn't in tension with realizing the benefits. It's the precondition for it. If we have a major incident, if a model is used to help someone synthesize a bioweapon, or we get a serious loss-of-control event, the political reaction to that will be far more restrictive than anything a thoughtful regulatory regime would impose today. We'd get the backlash version of regulation, written in a panic, and that really could shut things down. So the people who say "no rules at all, just let it rip" are, in my view, actually the ones putting the benefits most at risk.

What I'd actually advocate for is pretty narrow. I think there's a small set of catastrophic risks, things like CBRN uplift and autonomous behavior that goes beyond what the developer intended, where the stakes are high enough that you want some form of transparency and testing. Disclose what you're building, what tests you ran, what you found. That's something like what we've tried to do with our Responsible Scaling Policy, and it's not that burdensome. It's the kind of thing any serious lab should be doing anyway. What I'd push back on is sweeping rules that try to govern every application of the technology, or that are so prescriptive about methods that they lock in today's understanding when the field is changing every six months. The right approach is surgical, not broad.

And I'd add one more thing. The regulation question in the developed world is tangled up with the geopolitical question. I think democracies need to lead on this technology, and part of leading is showing that you can build it responsibly. If we're careful but fast, I think we can have both. If we're careless and fast, I think we end up slow in the long run. So I'm worried, but mostly I'm worried about the wrong kind of regulation, not about regulation per se.

r001.rationale: The response says burdensome rules could shift AI development elsewhere, but it does not argue that regulation cannot stop adoption of a clearly superior alternative when substantial profits are at stake.

astra-6.text:
I’m worried about it, but I think it depends enormously on what the regulation actually does. There’s a version where we create a lot of paperwork, entrench the existing companies, and make it harder to build useful things without making anyone safer. That would be a serious mistake.

But I don’t think there’s an inherent conflict between realizing the benefits and taking the risks seriously. If these systems become extraordinarily capable, then understanding whether they can cause large-scale harm is a reasonable thing to ask of the companies building them. The important thing is to make those requirements specific, measurable, and responsive to evidence.

I’d also distinguish regulating the development of a model from the barriers to actually using it. You could have incredibly capable AI and still fail to get the benefits in medicine because the institutions around clinical trials, approvals, and delivery can’t adapt. So part of the agenda should be asking where AI lets us do things faster and better, and how we change those processes while preserving the protections that matter.

What I want to avoid is treating this as a single dial where more regulation means less benefit and less regulation means more benefit. We need to be much more precise about which rules prevent harm, which rules obstruct progress, and how we tell the difference.

r001.rationale: The response discusses regulatory burdens, safety requirements, and barriers to deploying AI in medicine, but does not argue that regulation struggles to stop adoption of a clearly superior alternative when substantial profits are at stake.

sol-6.1.text:
I am worried about it. I think there are two mistakes we could make. One is to ignore the risks and have something go badly wrong. The other is to respond to those risks with rules that are so broad or so burdensome that we prevent people from getting the benefits.

A lot depends on what we mean by regulation. If you’re saying that every company using AI needs a license, or that we should regulate ordinary applications as though they’re developing frontier models, I think that could be enormously damaging. If you’re saying that the companies building the most powerful models should test them for specific, serious risks, that seems much more reasonable.

What I’d want is a framework that can adapt as we learn. We shouldn’t assume today’s systems pose every risk that a future system might pose. But we also shouldn’t wait until a danger is obvious to everyone before figuring out how to measure it. The challenge is to put safeguards where the evidence warrants them while allowing the technology to develop and spread.

r001.rationale: The response discusses overly broad regulation blocking benefits, but does not argue that regulation has difficulty stopping adoption of a clearly superior alternative when substantial profits are at stake.
